query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build substrate during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder will reduce the thermal gradients that cause segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation and thereby improve the mechanical integrity of the fabricated parts.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock that, when processed through conventional or standard LPBF conditions, tends to develop compositional segregation, high residual thermal stresses, and process‐induced defects.
generation.intervention: Apply an in situ substrate preheating step (e.g., raising the build platform to a moderate elevated temperature) during LPBF processing.
generation.conditions: LPBF processing under standard industrial parameters at ambient conditions, with the only change being a controlled, moderate preheat of the build platform (tentatively in the range of 300–500 °C). Comparison measurements are made at room temperature on samples produced with and without preheating.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduced temperature gradient across the deposited layers that leads to a more uniform solidification process, thereby diminishing the tendency for element segregation and the development of high residual stresses and associated defects (e.g., microcracks, lack-of-fusion porosity).
generation.mechanism: By elevating the substrate temperature, the cooling rate is moderated, which minimizes the thermal contraction mismatch between successive layers. This reduction in thermal gradients helps to achieve a more homogeneous microstructure with improved metallurgical bonding, fewer stress concentrations, and reduced defect sites.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventionally fabricated or non-preheated LPBF samples, the preheated samples should exhibit lower residual stresses, reduced compositional segregation at grain boundaries, and fewer defects. Mechanically, this should manifest as an increase in yield strength and ductility, leading to overall improved mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: AlCrFeNiSi parts produced via conventional LPBF or bulk fabrication without any substrate preheating, which tend to exhibit notable segregation, high residual stresses, and defects that impair mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable under LPBF processing conditions with typical layer thickness and build atmospheres. The benefits are expected provided that the preheat temperature is optimized; excessively high temperatures might lead to grain coarsening or other adverse microstructural changes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal preheat temperature and its quantitative impact on the mechanical properties remain to be determined; experimental calibration is necessary to balance improved thermal management with any potential grain growth effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi specimens using LPBF: one set with standard processing and another set with an elevated build substrate preheat (within a predetermined, moderate temperature range). Evaluate the specimens using microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM with EDS) to assess segregation and defect formation, X-ray diffraction or other stress measurement methods for residual stresses, and mechanical testing (tensile, hardness) for integrity.
measurements: Microstructural homogeneity (segregation and defect density via SEM/EDS)
Residual stress levels (via XRD stress analysis)
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in microstructural homogeneity, reduced residual stress, or enhanced mechanical performance relative to the standard specimens, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Multi-component alloys containing Co, Cr, Ni and other elements have attracted attention recently []. Equiatomic CoCrNi MEAs in particular demonstrate high strength and ductility at low temperatures []. CoCrNi MEAs are typically manufactured by casting and powder metallurgy, yielding a room temperature yield strength of only 360 MPa. Higher mechanical properties require additional processing like rolling, heat treatment and high pressure torsion []. Mechanical alloying (MA) combined with spark plasma sintering (SPS) can also produce CoCrNi MEAs with improved mechanics []. Traditional casting has some shortcomings such as low solidification rate, element segregation and rough casting microstructure, which requires heat treatment to optimize the structure. Compared to traditional casting, LAM can fabricate complex geometries []. LAM enables high cooling rates and temperature gradients, yielding refined solid solution phases and microstructures well-suited for high quality CoCrNi MEAs. Research on CoCrNi MEAs with LAM remains limited. There are many articles on LAM of CoCrNi MEAs. but there are very few articles on HSLAM CoCrNi MEAs. Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a disruptive additive manufacturing (AM) technology with the potential to revolutionize the fabrication of geometrically complex products from metal powders, overcoming the limitations of conventional processing methods [,]. Its ultra-high cooling rate of 103–108 K/s during non-equilibrium solidification effectively inhibits grain growth and the segregation of alloying elements within metal materials, which are challenging to achieve through conventional processing methods []. LPBF enables the production of metallic materials with microstructures characterized by highly heterogeneous grain geometries, sub-grain dislocation structures, and chemical segregation [,], thus resulting in exceptional mechanical properties.

Additive manufacturing (AM) is rapidly emerging as a pivotal technology for industrial part production due to its ability to create intricate shapes through computer-assisted layer-by-layer part construction. In metal AM, a broad, ever-expanding technology landscape has emerged with varying degrees of adoption in industry. While various AM technologies exist, liquid-mediated metal AM, notably Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), has garnered significant interest in industry and academia due to its potential to produce high-quality parts. L-PBF’s quality relies on understanding the interplay between process parameters, material properties, and solidification conditions. Traditional alloy design primarily targets specific manufacturing routes and often overlooks the unique demands of additive manufacturing (AM). In AM, designing alloys requires optimizing both chemistry and processing conditions simultaneously to minimize defects and enhance reliability. Conventional approaches first focus on achieving target properties and then on developing scalable processing methods.
